questions.stem: The killing of one's father is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'pater' = father + 'caedere' = to kill. Matricide = mother, fratricide = brother, filicide = one's child. All four distractors come from the same cluster — a student must know the whole family to answer securely.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of one's brother is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'frater' = brother. Sororicide = sister, parricide = parent or close relative, homicide = any human. Cain-and-Abel is the archetypal fratricide.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of a king is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'rex, regis' = king. Compare with tyrannicide (tyrant) and deicide (a god). The moral-framing trap: historians sometimes use 'tyrannicide' to praise the same act, 'regicide' to condemn it.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The deliberate killing of a racial or ethnic group is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'genos' = race / kind + L. 'caedere' = to kill. Coined by Polish jurist Raphael Lemkin (1944) in the context of the Holocaust. Tested often in current-affairs + vocab overlaps.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of one's own wife is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'uxor' = wife. Its counterpart is mariticide (killing of one's husband, L. 'maritus'). Both appear in legal-vocabulary papers.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of an infant is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'infans' = unable to speak, a baby. Distinguish from filicide (killing of one's OWN child, at any age). A classic exam pair.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A substance used to kill insects is called a:
questions.explanation: L. 'pestis' = plague/pest. Herbicide targets plants/weeds; fungicide targets fungi; germicide targets micro-organisms. The -cide root unifies them all — learn one, recognise all.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of a tyrant by a citizen is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'tyrannos' = absolute ruler. Often used in political philosophy (Locke, classical debate on rightful resistance). Regicide names the act (killing a king) without the moral framing.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The large-scale destruction of the environment is termed:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'oikos' = house, habitat (also root of ecology, economy). Ecocide is an emerging legal concept — proposed as a fifth international crime alongside genocide. Appears in modern editorial vocabulary.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The killing of one's own mother is called:
questions.explanation: L. 'mater' = mother. Pair with patricide to set the baseline; add filicide (child), uxoricide (wife), sororicide (sister) and the cluster is complete.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which of the following terms refers to a chemical agent designed to kill or suppress unwanted plants and weeds?

options.option_text: Fungicide — a chemical used to kill harmful fungi and mould
Herbicide — a chemical substance that kills plants and weeds
Rodenticide — a substance used to eliminate rats and mice
Germicide — an agent that destroys disease-causing microorganisms

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'herbicide' derives from Latin herba (plant) + caedere (to kill), meaning an agent that kills vegetation. Option A (fungicide) targets fungi, not plants. Option C (rodenticide) targets rodents. Option D (germicide) is for microorganisms. A common mix-up is confusing herbicide with fungicide when recalling agricultural chemicals.

questions.stem: The clinical and legal term for the deliberate act of taking one's own life is:

options.option_text: Homicide — the unlawful killing of another human being
Filicide — the killing of one's own child by a parent
Suicide — the deliberate act of ending one's own life
Senicide — the killing of elderly members within a community

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'suicide' comes from Latin sui (of oneself) + caedere (to kill). Option A (homicide) involves killing another person, not oneself. Option B (filicide) is a parent killing a child. Option D (senicide) refers to elimination of the elderly — a practice documented in certain ancient societies.

questions.stem: The deliberate killing of one's own sister is specifically termed:

options.option_text: Fratricide — the deliberate killing of one's own brother
Sororicide — the deliberate act of killing one's own sister
Avunculicide — the deliberate killing of one's own uncle
Filicide — the killing of one's own son or daughter

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'sororicide' derives from Latin soror (sister) + caedere (to kill). The most tempting distractor is A (fratricide, from frater = brother), which is the male-sibling parallel. Avunculicide (from avunculus = maternal uncle) and filicide (from filius = son) are different family-relation -cides entirely.

questions.stem: Which term precisely describes a parent's act of killing their own child, regardless of the child's age at the time?

options.option_text: Neonaticide — the killing of a newborn within 24 hours of birth
Infanticide — the killing of any infant under one year of age
Prolicide — the destruction of one's offspring or future progeny
Filicide — the killing of one's own child regardless of the child's age

questions.explanation: D is correct because 'filicide' (Latin filius/filia = son/daughter) applies to a parent killing a child of any age. Option B (infanticide) is age-restricted to infants and need not involve the parent. Option A (neonaticide) is even narrower — only within 24 hours of birth. The most tempting wrong answer is B because infanticide was already encountered in prior study, but it lacks the parent-specificity that filicide carries.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms specifically denotes the killing of one's own husband?

options.option_text: Mariticide — the killing of one's own husband by the spouse
Avunculicide — the killing of one's own uncle or male relative
Patricide — the deliberate killing of one's own father figure
Prolicide — the destruction or deliberate killing of one's own offspring

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'mariticide' derives from Latin maritus (husband) + caedere (to kill). This is the husband-killing counterpart to uxoricide (wife-killing). Option C (patricide, from pater = father) is the most tempting distractor since it also involves killing a senior male family member. Avunculicide (uncle) and prolicide (offspring) involve entirely different relationships.

questions.stem: The term 'vaticide' derives from the Latin word 'vates'. It refers to the killing of:

options.option_text: A sacred cow or bovine animal revered in religious traditions
A divine or godlike being worshipped in classical mythology
A prophet, seer, or divinely inspired sacred poet
A sovereign ruler or chieftain of an ancient tribal people

questions.explanation: C is correct because in classical Latin, 'vates' meant a prophet, seer, or inspired poet — figures like oracles. Option B (divine being) is the most tempting error because candidates confuse vaticide with deicide (from Latin deus = god). Option D (ruler) is confused with regicide. Option A is a phonetic trap on 'vat', which has no Latin connection to this word.

questions.stem: In political psychology and Cold War literature, the term 'menticide' is used to describe:

options.option_text: The clinical elimination of patients with severe mental disorders
The deliberate destruction of a person's mind and free will
A surgical procedure aimed at removing diseased brain tissue
The mass killing of intellectuals within an authoritarian state

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'menticide' (Latin mens = mind + caedere = to kill) was coined by psychiatrist Joost Meerloo to describe systematic brainwashing, forced confessions, and psychological manipulation used to destroy a captive's will — famously analysed in the context of Soviet show trials. Option D is the most plausible distractor because it conflates menticide with politicide or the killing of intellectuals, but menticide targets the mind of a living person, not their physical body.
